articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M Tourism Contract Renewed Without Competitive Bid
articles.dek: County commissioners extended Visit Pensacola's marketing agreement last month with minimal public discussion. Records show the decision bypassed standard procurement review.
brief: Escambia County commissioners approved a $2.3 million annual contract extension with Visit Pensacola on May 14 without issuing a competitive bid or conducting a formal procurement review.
The five-year agreement, which governs how tourist development tax revenue is spent on destination marketing, was renewed through a consent agenda item that received no public comment.

County procurement policy requires competitive bidding for contracts exceeding $50,000, but tourism marketing agreements have been treated as exempt under a 2018 administrative interpretation that critics say lacks legal foundation.
articles.body:
The contract appeared on page 47 of a 312-page consent agenda packet. No commissioner pulled it for separate discussion. No member of the public spoke on the item. The vote took four seconds.

That's how Escambia County renewed its $2.3 million annual agreement with Visit Pensacola last month—a five-year extension worth $11.5 million in tourist development tax revenue that will fund beach advertising campaigns, travel industry trade shows and promotional videos through 2031.

Records obtained by The Flightline show the contract bypassed the county's standard procurement process. No request for proposals was issued. No competing bids were solicited. No evaluation committee scored alternative vendors.

County Administrator Wes Moreno said the renewal fell under an administrative exception for "ongoing service relationships" that his office has applied to tourism marketing since 2018.

"Visit Pensacola has been our destination marketing organization for over a decade," Moreno said in a written statement. "There's continuity value in that relationship that a competitive process wouldn't capture."

The Exception That Swallowed the Rule

Escambia County's procurement code requires competitive bidding for any contract exceeding $50,000. The rule exists to prevent favoritism, ensure taxpayer value and give local vendors a fair shot at public work.

But the code includes a narrow exception: contracts may bypass competitive review when "the nature of the service makes competition impractical." The original intent, according to a 2003 staff memo, was to cover situations like emergency repairs or specialized professional services where only one qualified vendor exists.

In 2018, then-County Administrator Jack Brown issued an internal guidance memo extending that exception to destination marketing agreements. His reasoning: tourism promotion requires "market-specific expertise and brand continuity" that competitive bidding would disrupt.

No commissioner voted on that interpretation. It never appeared on a public agenda. Brown simply directed the procurement office to treat tourism contracts as exempt.

"That's an administrative decision that rewrote procurement policy without elected approval," said Dana Morrison, a former county budget analyst who now consults for Florida municipalities. "It's the kind of thing that should have gone to the board."

Brown retired in 2021. His memo remains in effect.

What the Contract Funds

Visit Pensacola operates as the county's official destination marketing organization. The nonprofit—technically a 501(c)(6) trade association—receives roughly 40% of Escambia County's annual tourist development tax collections, which totaled $5.8 million in fiscal year 2025.

Under the renewed agreement, Visit Pensacola will continue managing the county's tourism brand, running advertising campaigns targeting drive markets in Alabama, Georgia and Louisiana, attending travel industry conferences and producing promotional content.

The contract specifies performance metrics: website traffic targets, social media engagement benchmarks and annual visitor surveys. Visit Pensacola met or exceeded most metrics in its 2025 annual report, though the report was self-authored and not independently audited.

Visit Pensacola President Darien Schaefer said the organization's track record justified the direct renewal.

"We've delivered consistent results for Escambia County tourism," Schaefer said. "A competitive bid process would have cost the county six months of marketing momentum during peak planning season."

What Competitors Say

At least two marketing firms contacted by The Flightline said they would have submitted proposals if a bid had been issued.

Gulf Coast Marketing Solutions, a Fort Walton Beach agency that handles tourism promotion for several Florida municipalities, said it learned of the contract renewal only after the May 14 vote.

"We've pitched Escambia County before," said owner Michael Tran. "We were told there'd be an RFP eventually. Then we find out it's already done."

Tran said his firm has handled destination marketing for Walton County, Bay County and the city of Destin. He estimated Gulf Coast could deliver comparable services for 15% less than Visit Pensacola's current rate.

"Without a competitive process, there's no way to know if the county's getting the best value," Tran said.

A spokesperson for the Florida Association of Destination Marketing Organizations declined to comment on the Escambia contract specifically but said competitive bidding is "not standard practice" for DMO agreements statewide.

Commission Response

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said he was comfortable with the renewal process.

"Visit Pensacola knows our market," Bergosh said in an interview. "I don't see the benefit of putting this out to bid and potentially ending up with some outfit from Miami that doesn't understand Northwest Florida."

Asked whether the 2018 administrative exception should have required board approval, Bergosh said he would review the procurement code but added: "We rely on staff to make these determinations."

Commissioner Lumon May did not respond to requests for comment. Commissioners Steven Barry and Mike Kohler declined interviews, with their offices citing scheduling conflicts.

Commissioner Francesca Cunningham, elected in 2024, said she was unaware the contract had bypassed competitive review until contacted by The Flightline.

"I voted yes on the consent agenda," Cunningham said. "I should have looked more closely. This is the kind of thing that erodes public trust."

Transparency Questions

The contract renewal packet provided to commissioners contained Visit Pensacola's 2025 annual report, a draft of the new agreement and a one-paragraph staff summary recommending approval. It did not include any analysis of alternative vendors, cost comparisons or an explanation of why competitive bidding was waived.

County purchasing director Angela Rhodes said such analysis "wasn't required" under the 2018 guidance memo.

Morrison, the former budget analyst, said that's precisely the problem.

"When you exempt a $2.3 million contract from competitive review, you should at least document why," she said. "The public record should show the county considered alternatives and made an informed choice. Here, there's nothing."

Tourist development tax revenue comes from a 5% surcharge on short-term rentals—hotels, vacation homes, Airbnbs. The tax is paid by visitors, but it's public money once collected, subject to the same accountability standards as property taxes or sales taxes.

"People assume this is hotel money that doesn't affect them," Morrison said. "But it's revenue the county could spend on beach renourishment, parking, lifeguards. Every dollar to Visit Pensacola is a dollar not going somewhere else."

What Happens Next

The renewed contract runs through September 30, 2031. It includes annual renewal options and performance review clauses, but no provision for rebidding during the five-year term.

Cunningham said she plans to raise the procurement exception issue at a future board meeting.

"I'm not saying Visit Pensacola is doing a bad job," she said. "I'm saying we should have a process that proves we're getting the best deal. Right now, we're just taking it on faith."

Moreno, the county administrator, said he would "welcome board guidance" on whether tourism contracts should be subject to competitive bidding in the future.

"If commissioners want to change the policy, we'll change the policy," he said. "But they'd need to understand the operational implications."

The next county commission meeting is scheduled for June 18. As of press time, the agenda had not been published.

articles.label: Analysis
articles.headline: Downtown's Empty Storefronts: A Block-by-Block Count of Palafox Vacancies
articles.dek: Six months after two major restaurants closed, The Flightline walked every block of the downtown core. What we found challenges the narrative of a retail boom.
brief: A physical survey of Palafox Street from Main to Garden found 23 vacant storefronts in the downtown commercial core
The vacancy rate has increased from roughly 8% to 14% since December 2024, contradicting city promotional materials
Five of the vacancies are former restaurants that closed within the past 18 months
articles.body:
The paper sign in the window at 21 S. Palafox has been there so long the sun has bleached the edges yellow. "Coming Soon," it still reads. The space has been empty for fourteen months.

On a Tuesday morning in early June, The Flightline walked every block of Palafox Street from Main Street to Garden Street, clipboard in hand. We counted storefronts. We noted vacancy signs, dark windows, locked doors at midday. We photographed what we found.

The count: 23 vacant commercial spaces in the downtown core. That's out of roughly 165 ground-floor storefronts along the corridor, a vacancy rate of approximately 14%.

Six months ago, when Iron and Wren Kitchen + Cocktails shuttered after three years on South Palafox, city officials called it an isolated closure. When Broussard's Cajun Cuisine followed two weeks later, Mayor D.C. Reeves told the Pensacola News Journal that downtown remained "as vibrant as ever."

The numbers tell a different story.

What We Found

The methodology was simple: walk every block, count every space. A storefront counted as vacant if it had no active business, regardless of whether it displayed a "For Lease" sign. Spaces under active construction with visible permits were noted separately.

The results broke down by block:

From Main Street to Romana Street, the southern stretch closest to the bay, we counted four vacancies. Two of these are former restaurants. One has been empty since a gift shop closed in early 2024.

The 0-100 block of South Palafox, historically the most desirable retail stretch, had six vacancies. This includes the former Iron and Wren space at 32 S. Palafox, which remains dark with no visible leasing activity. A former jewelry store at 78 S. Palafox has been vacant for at least two years according to neighboring business owners.

North of Garden Street, the count reached thirteen vacancies in a four-block stretch. Several of these spaces show no signs of active marketing.

The Official Numbers

The Downtown Improvement Board's most recent quarterly report, published in April, cited a "healthy commercial occupancy rate" without providing a specific percentage. The report highlighted seven new business openings in the first quarter of 2026.

DIB Executive Director Lori Chabries did not respond to two emails and a phone message requesting comment for this article.

The city's Office of Economic Development lists downtown Pensacola as having a 92% occupancy rate on its website, a figure that appears to date from 2024. Economic Development Director Keith Wilkins said via email that the office relies on DIB data and does not conduct independent surveys.

"We're confident in the overall trajectory of downtown development," Wilkins wrote. "Individual vacancies are a normal part of any commercial district's evolution."

What Business Owners Say

Michael Chen has operated a men's clothing store on South Palafox for eleven years. He's watched the block change around him.

"Used to be you couldn't get a space down here," Chen said. "Landlords had waiting lists. Now I see the same 'For Lease' signs month after month."

Chen said his own sales are down roughly 15% from 2024. He attributes part of that to reduced foot traffic from the restaurant closures.

"People came downtown to eat, then they'd walk around, maybe stop in a few shops," he said. "Fewer restaurants means fewer people walking past my window."

Not everyone shares that assessment. Amanda Rodriguez opened a vintage furniture store on North Palafox in February. She said she secured favorable lease terms precisely because of the vacancies.

"My landlord was motivated," Rodriguez said. "I got six months at reduced rent. That wouldn't have happened two years ago."

She added that she's seen steady customer traffic since opening. "I think there's still demand for interesting retail downtown. But you have to offer something people can't get at Cordova Mall."

The Restaurant Question

Five of the 23 vacancies are former restaurant spaces. Beyond Iron and Wren and Broussard's, the list includes a sandwich shop that closed in late 2024, a breakfast spot that lasted eight months and a seafood restaurant that shuttered during the 2025 off-season and never reopened.

Restaurant industry observers point to several factors: rising food costs, difficulty finding staff and lease rates that climbed during the post-pandemic boom.

Jake Morrison operated a food truck for four years before opening a brick-and-mortar location on Palafox in 2023. He closed it after eighteen months.

"The rent was $4,200 a month for 1,400 square feet," Morrison said. "That's triple-net, so I'm also paying property taxes, insurance, maintenance. To make that work, I needed to do $35,000 a month minimum. We were doing maybe $28,000 on a good month."

Morrison said his landlord offered no rent reduction when he asked. "They said they could find another tenant. Maybe they can. But the space is still empty eight months later."

The Construction Factor

Three spaces along Palafox are currently under renovation with active building permits. A fourth, the former location of a women's boutique, had construction materials visible through the window but no posted permit.

Two of the permitted renovations are for restaurant concepts. One is a expansion of an existing bar into an adjacent space. The other is a new breakfast and lunch spot from operators who previously ran a successful food truck.

The third permitted renovation is for a satellite location of a Destin-based real estate office.

These pending openings will reduce the vacancy count when completed, likely in late summer or fall. But they don't fully offset the closures of the past eighteen months.

Comparing the Data

Establishing a historical baseline is difficult. The DIB's quarterly reports from 2023 and 2024 do not include specific vacancy counts or occupancy percentages.

However, a December 2024 promotional document from the city's tourism office stated that downtown Palafox had "fewer than 15 vacant storefronts." If accurate, that would represent an increase of eight vacancies in eighteen months.

The Flightline requested the underlying data for that figure through a public records request. The city responded that no such data exists. "The figure was an estimate based on staff observation," wrote communications director Patricia Holmes.

A 2021 report from the University of West Florida's Haas Center found a downtown commercial vacancy rate of approximately 8%. Using comparable methodology, our count suggests that rate has risen to 14%.

What It Means

A 14% vacancy rate is not catastrophic. Commercial districts across Florida show similar or higher numbers. Panama City's downtown corridor has struggled with vacancies exceeding 20% since Hurricane Michael. Even thriving districts in larger cities typically maintain vacancy rates of 5-10%.

But the trend line matters. Downtown Pensacola invested heavily in streetscaping, parking and promotional efforts over the past decade. The narrative from city hall has been one of continuous growth and increasing desirability.

The empty storefronts along Palafox complicate that narrative. They suggest a market that has cooled, or at minimum stabilized, after years of expansion.

Chen, the clothing store owner, put it simply: "Nobody's saying downtown is dying. But pretending everything's perfect doesn't help anybody. We need honest conversations about rent, about parking, about what kind of businesses can actually survive here."

The Flightline will conduct a follow-up survey in December to track changes in downtown's commercial occupancy. We welcome tips from readers about business openings, closures or other developments along the Palafox corridor.

articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors. It Also Brings Questions About Who Pays.
articles.dek: The July airshow generates millions for local businesses. But city and county taxpayers cover traffic control, emergency services and cleanup—costs that have never been fully disclosed.
brief: Blue Angels Homecoming draws an estimated 200,000 spectators and generates $25-30 million in local economic activity annually
Neither Escambia County nor the City of Pensacola has published a full accounting of public costs for traffic control, emergency services and infrastructure
Other military airshow host cities require event organizers to reimburse municipal costs or cap public expenditures
articles.body:
The porta-potties arrive first. Then the barricades, the traffic cones, the deputy sheriffs pulling double shifts. By the Wednesday before Blue Angels Homecoming, Pensacola Beach looks like a small city preparing for a siege.

For three days each July, an estimated 200,000 people pack the sugar-white sand to watch the Navy's flight demonstration squadron perform overhead. Hotel rooms from Perdido Key to Navarre sell out months in advance. Restaurants run out of grouper. The Pensacola Bay Area Convention and Visitors Bureau estimates the event generates between $25 and $30 million in direct economic activity.

What no one can say with certainty is how much it costs the public to make that weekend happen.

The Money Nobody Tracks

The Flightline submitted public records requests to Escambia County, Santa Rosa County, the City of Pensacola, the Town of Pensacola Beach and the Santa Rosa Island Authority seeking itemized costs associated with Blue Angels Homecoming for the past five years.

The responses painted an incomplete picture.

Escambia County provided partial figures showing the Sheriff's Office logged approximately 2,400 overtime hours during the 2025 event weekend at an estimated cost of $156,000. The county's public works department could not separate Homecoming-related expenses from its general summer operations budget.

"We don't have a line item for that," said county spokesperson Alicia Herrera. "It's just part of what we do."

Santa Rosa County reported spending $43,000 on traffic control and emergency medical standby for the Pensacola Beach portions of the event in 2025. The Town of Gulf Breeze, which absorbs spillover traffic on Highway 98, does not track event-specific costs at all.

The City of Pensacola, which hosts the Thursday night airshow rehearsal over Pensacola Bay and the accompanying downtown crowds, estimated its 2025 costs at $78,000. That figure included police overtime, sanitation and Parks and Recreation staff but excluded any portion of fire department readiness.

Taken together, the documented public expenditures exceed $277,000 annually. The actual number is almost certainly higher.

Who Should Pay

Blue Angels Homecoming differs from most large events in one critical respect: it has no private promoter.

The airshow itself is a Navy operation. NAS Pensacola opens its gates to the public. The Blue Angels Foundation, a nonprofit, handles some logistics and hospitality. But there is no ticketed venue, no central organizer writing checks.

"It's a community event," said retired Navy Capt. Mark Thompson, who served as Blue Angels commanding officer from 2018 to 2019. "The whole region benefits. That's the point."

Other cities have taken a different approach. Fort Lauderdale, which hosts the Blue Angels for an annual beach airshow, requires the private event organizer to reimburse the city for all police, fire and public works costs. Organizers pay roughly $400,000 annually.

In El Centro, California, where the Blue Angels train each winter, Imperial County caps its public safety contribution and bills the Navy for costs above that threshold.

Escambia County has never proposed either model.

The Accountability Gap

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said he had never seen a comprehensive cost analysis of Homecoming.

"That's a fair question," Bergosh said. "I'd want to look at what other communities do. But I also don't want to kill something that brings this much positive attention to our area."

Commissioner Lumon May, who represents downtown Pensacola neighborhoods, said constituents have raised concerns about the burden on local services.

"When you've got every deputy working overtime and ambulances staged on the beach, somebody's paying for that," May said. "It shouldn't be a mystery who."

The Navy declined to comment on whether NAS Pensacola reimburses any local government costs. A spokesperson for the Blue Angels Foundation said the organization "works closely with local partners" but does not have financial agreements with municipal governments.

A Question of Transparency

The economic benefits of Homecoming are real. Hotels report their highest occupancy rates of the year. Restaurants hire extra staff. The tourism marketing value of national television coverage is difficult to quantify but clearly substantial.

Whether those benefits justify unlimited public expenditure is a policy question local officials have declined to ask publicly.

What is not in dispute is that taxpayers deserve to know the answer.

"If it's worth doing, it's worth tracking," said Amy Patterson, a retired accountant who lives in Gulf Breeze and has attended Homecoming for 30 years. "I'm not saying don't do it. I'm saying tell us what it costs. That's just basic."

The 2026 Blue Angels Homecoming is scheduled for July 9-11. Planning is already underway. Once again, no one is adding up the bill.
